content: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a condition characterized by both metabolic and reproductive dysfunctions, affecting approximately 5% to 15% of women of reproductive age. Various Western medical treatments have been proposed to address subfertility associated with PCOS, including oral contraceptives, insulin sensitizers, and laparoscopic ovarian drilling (LOD). Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) has also been used for decades as a potential treatment for subfertility in women with PCOS and is being considered as an alternative therapeutic option. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of CHM in treating subfertile women with PCOS. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to June 2, 2020. Additional searches included trial registries, reference lists of included studies, and consultations with experts in the field. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing CHM to placebo, no treatment, or conventional Western therapies were included in the analysis. Eight RCTs involving 609 participants were included in the review. The studies compared CHM to clomiphene, CHM combined with clomiphene versus clomiphene alone (with or without ethinyloestradiol cyproterone acetate (EE/CPA)), CHM combined with follicle aspiration and ovulation induction versus follicle aspiration and ovulation induction alone, and CHM combined with LOD versus LOD alone. The overall certainty of the evidence for most comparisons was rated as very low. None of the included studies reported live birth rates, which was the primary outcome of interest. Most studies reported secondary outcomes, and only one study provided data on adverse events. In trials comparing CHM to clomiphene (with or without LOD in both groups), the effect of CHM on pregnancy rates was uncertain (odds ratio (OR) 1.41, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.63 to 3.19; I² = 28%; 3 studies, 140 participants; very low certainty evidence). If the pregnancy rate with clomiphene is assumed to be 21.5%, the pregnancy rate with CHM would range between 14.7% and 46.7%. No adverse event data were reported in these studies. When CHM combined with clomiphene was compared to clomiphene alone (with or without EE/CPA), there was low-certainty evidence suggesting a higher pregnancy rate in the CHM plus clomiphene group (OR 3.06, 95% CI 2.05 to 4.55; I² = 10%; 6 studies, 470 participants). If the pregnancy rate with clomiphene alone is assumed to be 31.5%, the pregnancy rate with CHM plus clomiphene would range between 48.5% and 67.7%. Again, no adverse event data were reported. In a single trial comparing CHM combined with follicle aspiration and ovulation induction to follicle aspiration and ovulation induction alone, the effect of CHM on pregnancy rates was uncertain (OR 1.62, 95% CI 0.46 to 5.68; 1 study, 44 women; very low certainty evidence). If the pregnancy rate with follicle aspiration and ovulation induction alone is assumed to be 29.2%, the pregnancy rate with CHM would range between 15.9% and 70%. Reported adverse events included severe luteinized unruptured follicle syndrome (LUFS) (Peto OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.06 to 6.14; very low certainty evidence), ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) (Peto OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.00 to 8.19; very low certainty evidence), and multiple pregnancy (Peto OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.06 to 6.14; very low certainty evidence). If the risks of LUFS, OHSS, and multiple pregnancy with follicle aspiration and ovulation induction alone are assumed to be 8.3%, 4.2%, and 8.3%, respectively, the risks with CHM would range between 0.5% and 35.8%, 0% and 26.3%, and 0.5% and 35.8%, respectively. In a single trial comparing CHM combined with LOD to LOD alone, the effect of CHM on pregnancy rates was also uncertain (OR 3.50, 95% CI 0.72 to 17.09; 1 study, 30 women; very low certainty evidence). If the pregnancy rate with LOD alone is assumed to be 40%, the pregnancy rate with CHM plus LOD would range between 32.4% and 91.9%. No adverse event data were reported. Overall, the certainty of the evidence for all comparisons and outcomes was very low. The main limitations included the lack of data on live birth rates and adverse events, insufficient detail in study methods, and imprecision due to low event rates and wide confidence intervals. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of CHM for subfertile women with PCOS. No data are available on live birth rates, and the effect of CHM on pregnancy rates remains uncertain. While the addition of CHM to clomiphene may improve pregnancy rates, the evidence for this outcome is limited and of low certainty. Furthermore, there is insufficient evidence to determine the safety of CHM. Future research should focus on well-designed, rigorously conducted RCTs that prioritize live birth rates and safety outcomes.
